phrases.translation: Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with a gift already given. God has granted the Prophet a clear victory, and the word for victory is explained as a judgement, a decision made in his favour that is plain to anyone who hears it. It is called clear because it settles the dispute with those who opposed him. The reports identify this victory as the truce at Ḥudaybiya, which looked like a setback and was named a triumph, and the rest of the surah explains why.

phrases.translation: so that Allah may forgive you for your past and future shortcomings,
phrases.explanation: The purpose of the victory is stated first. God forgives the Prophet what came before of his shortcomings and what came after, and the verse is explained as a reward for the gratitude he would show. One report has him standing in prayer until his feet swelled, and answering that he should surely be a grateful servant when asked why he did so. The verse is a promise attached to that gratitude, not a licence to be careless.

phrases.translation: perfect His favour upon you, guide you along the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: The favours named next follow in order. God completes His favour on him by giving him victory over his enemy, raising his name in this world and forgiving him in the next. He also guides him on a straight path, showing him the way of a religion in which there is no crookedness, leading directly to his Lord's good pleasure. The verse describes the completion of a favour rather than the start of one.

phrases.translation: and so that Allah will help you tremendously
phrases.explanation: The promise of help is then stated in its own verse. God will help him against all who oppose him, with a help that no overpowering force can overcome and no repelling hand can push back. The strength is God's and the victory is His gift, so the help cannot be undone by the numbers against him. The three verses together form a single sentence: the victory, the forgiveness, and the help.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who sent down serenity upon the hearts of the believers so that they may increase even more in their faith.
phrases.explanation: The verse names what God sent down into the hearts of the believers. It is serenity, explained here as calm and quiet of soul, and it was directed toward faith and toward the truth the Prophet brought. The purpose is that they might add faith to faith, and one report explains the increase as the obligations that came one after another, prayer then fasting then alms then pilgrimage, each accepted in turn. Each new command found them ready.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The verse turns from the hearts to the armies. To God belong the forces of the heavens and the earth, and they are described as helpers through whom He takes vengeance on whom He wills of His enemies. He is All-Knowing, knowing what exists before it exists and what His creatures will do, and All-Wise in His governance. The mention of the armies answers any fear that the believers were few.

phrases.translation: So He may admit believing men and women into Gardens under which rivers flow—to stay there forever—and absolve them of their sins.
phrases.explanation: The purpose continues with the reward laid up for the believers. God will admit believing men and women into gardens beneath which the rivers flow, to remain there forever, and He will remove their evil deeds from them. The removal is explained as being done through the good deeds they perform out of gratitude. The men and the women are named separately so that no one supposes the promise is for one group alone.

phrases.translation: And that is a supreme achievement in the sight of Allah
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with a verdict on what has been promised. Admission into the gardens and the wiping away of evil deeds is, with God, a supreme achievement, a success in what they hoped for and a deliverance from what they feared. The words are said to be the answer to the believers who asked what was in the victory for them after the Prophet was told of his forgiveness.

phrases.translation: Also ˹so that˺ He may punish hypocrite men and women and polytheistic men and women, who harbour evil thoughts of Allah.
phrases.explanation: The other side of the victory is then named. God will punish hypocrite men and women and polytheist men and women, the ones who think evil thoughts about God. Their thought is that He will never help the Prophet and the believers, and that His word will never be raised above the word of those who deny Him. The verse puts the two groups together because the same doubt was in both.

phrases.translation: May ill-fate befall them! Allah is displeased with them. He has condemned them and prepared for them Hell. What an evil destination
phrases.explanation: The curse is then pronounced on them. May the evil turn befall them, meaning the turn of punishment that comes round upon them, and God is angry with them, has removed them from His mercy and prepared Hell for them. The question that closes names it an evil destination. The reciters differ over the vowel of one word in the curse, and both forms carry the same sense of evil.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belong the forces of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The verse repeats the statement about the armies, now as a closing word on the two groups. To God belong the forces of the heavens and the earth, and if He commands them against His enemies they destroy them and hasten in obedience to Him. He is Almighty, with a might nothing can overpower, and All-Wise in His disposal of what He made. The repetition is placed after the promise and the curse so that both rest on the same power.

phrases.translation: Indeed, ˹O Prophet,˺ We have sent you as a witness, a deliverer of good news, and a warner
phrases.explanation: The surah turns to the Prophet's own office. He is sent as a witness over his community concerning the answer they gave to the message, and as a bringer of good news of the Garden to those who obey, and as a warner of God's punishment to those who turn away. The three roles are named in one verse, and each answers a different response he would meet. The witness is not a prosecutor but one who will testify to what he delivered.

phrases.translation: so that you ˹believers˺ may have faith in Allah and His Messenger, support and honour him,
phrases.explanation: The purpose of the sending is then given. The believers are to have faith in God and His messenger, to support him and to honour him. The words for support and honour are explained as strengthening through help, exalting and venerating, and one report says the support meant fighting alongside him with the sword. The two together cover the hand and the heart, since the message is defended by action and held in esteem by reverence.

phrases.translation: and glorify Allah morning and evening
phrases.explanation: The last clause turns from the messenger to God. They are to glorify Him morning and evening, which is explained as praying to Him at both ends of the day, and the pronoun refers to God alone and not to the messenger. Some readings make the whole verse a report about what people will do rather than a command to them, and both are accepted. The verse closes by putting the praise of God at the start and end of the day.

phrases.translation: Surely those who pledge allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ are actually pledging allegiance to Allah. Allah’s Hand is over theirs.
phrases.explanation: The verse concerns the pledge given at Ḥudaybiya, where the companions swore not to flee when they met the enemy. The oath to the Prophet is called an oath to God, since God guaranteed them the Garden if they kept it. The hand of God is over their hands, explained either as His hand over theirs in the pledging or as His power above their power in aiding His messenger. The pledge is a transaction with God rather than with a man.

phrases.translation: Whoever breaks their pledge, it will only be to their own loss. And whoever fulfils their pledge to Allah, He will grant them a great reward
phrases.explanation: The two outcomes of the pledge are then stated. Whoever breaks it breaks it only against himself, since he leaves the company of those to whom the Garden was promised, and the messenger needs no help from him because God is his helper either way. Whoever keeps what he promised God will be given a great reward, which one report names simply as the Garden. The verse leaves the loss on the breaker and the gain on the keeper.

phrases.translation: The nomadic Arabs, who stayed behind, will say to you ˹O Prophet˺, “We were preoccupied with our wealth and families, so ask for forgiveness for us.” They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts.
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to those who stayed behind. The nomadic Arabs who did not set out with the Prophet for the pilgrimage come to him on his return and offer an excuse: their wealth and their families kept them busy, so let him ask forgiveness for them. The verse adds that they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts, since they ask for pardon without repentance or regret for having stayed away. Their excuse is answered before it is accepted.

phrases.translation: Say, “Who then can stand between you and Allah in any way, if He intends harm or benefit for you? In fact, Allah is All-Aware of what you do
phrases.explanation: The reply puts the question back to them. If the Prophet asked forgiveness for them and God then willed their destruction or the loss of their wealth and families, or willed benefit for them instead, who could stand between them and Him in any way? No one can repel what God wills, whether of good or of evil. The verse then says that God is well acquainted with what they do, and that nothing they conceal is hidden from Him.

phrases.translation: The truth is: you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again. And that was made appealing in your hearts.
phrases.explanation: The verse gives the real reason they stayed behind. They did not remain at home out of concern for their affairs, but because they supposed that the messenger and the believers would never come back to their families, the enemy having finished them. That thought was made to seem fair to them, and the verse names it as an evil thought about God. What looked like an excuse was a judgement on God's promise.

phrases.translation: You harboured evil thoughts ˹about Allah˺, and ˹so˺ became a doomed people.”
phrases.explanation: The consequence is stated in the same breath. Because they harboured that thought they became a doomed people, and the word for doomed is explained as a people in whom there is no good, destroyed and fit for nothing. One report gives the word as meaning corrupt, another as meaning nothing that remains. The verse closes the account of those who stayed behind by showing that their excuse and their ruin had one root.

phrases.translation: And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger, then We surely have prepared for the disbelievers a blazing Fire
phrases.explanation: The verse states the other side of the same truth. Whoever does not believe in God and His messenger, whether from among the Bedouins or anyone else, has been given a different preparation: God has made ready for them all a blazing fire that will flare against them when they enter it. The word for blazing carries the sense of a fire stirred up and kindled. The verse names the unbelief plainly because the excuse of the previous verses had just been heard.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: The verse returns to the dominion of God over the heavens and the earth. Since the sovereignty is His, no one can prevent Him from punishing the hypocrites if they persist, or from forgiving them if He forgives. The verse is an invitation to those who lagged behind to repent before the door closes. Power over both outcomes belongs to the One who owns everything.

phrases.translation: He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The two names that follow make the invitation possible. God forgives whoever He wills and punishes whoever He wills, and He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful toward those who turn to Him. One report says the forgiveness covers those who repent of their sins and their disobedience, and that the mercy means He will not punish them after they have turned. The verse leaves the choice open and names the character of the One who receives the returning.

phrases.translation: Those who stayed behind will say, when you ˹believers˺ set out to take the spoils of war, “Let us accompany you.” They wish to change Allah’s promise.
phrases.explanation: The ones who stayed behind return to the scene. When the believers set out toward the spoils, meaning the spoils of Khaybar that God had promised to the people of Ḥudaybiya, they ask to come along. The verse says they wish to change God's word, since the promise had already assigned those spoils to those who were present at the pledge. Their request is not a change of heart but an attempt to claim what had been settled.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “You will not accompany us. This is what Allah has said before.”
phrases.explanation: The answer they receive is a refusal with a reason. They will not accompany the believers, and this is what God had said beforehand, since the spoils belong to the people of the pledge and they were not among them. One report has God stating the principle that the spoils are for the people of struggle. The verse makes the exclusion a matter of God's prior word rather than of the Prophet's preference.

phrases.translation: They will then say, “In fact, you are driven by jealousy against us!” The truth is: they can hardly comprehend
phrases.explanation: Their reply is an accusation. They say that the believers are driven by envy and are keeping them from a share of the spoils. The verse answers that they understood but little, since the question was never one of envy but of who had been promised the spoils. Their guess about the motive is easier for them than the truth about their own position. The verse lets their own words show how little they had taken in.

phrases.translation: Say to nomadic Arabs, who stayed behind, “You will be called ˹to fight˺ against a people of great might, who you will fight unless they submit.
phrases.explanation: The verse addresses the same people with a second summons. They will be called to fight a people of great might, and they will fight them until those people submit. The reports name Persia and Byzantium, or Hawazin and Thaqif at Hunayn, or Banu Hanifa, or the Romans, and one view holds that the summons has not yet come to pass. What the verse settles is that the called will meet a hard fight, not an easy one.

phrases.translation: If you then obey, Allah will grant you a fine reward. But if you turn away as you did before, He will inflict upon you a painful punishment.”
phrases.explanation: The two outcomes are then stated. If they obey when they are called, God will give them a fine reward, which one report names as the Garden. If they turn away as they turned away before, when they failed to march with the Prophet to Mecca, He will inflict a painful punishment on them, and that is the punishment of the Fire. The verse leaves no middle position between answering and refusing.

phrases.translation: There is no blame on the blind, or the disabled, or the sick ˹for staying behind˺.
phrases.explanation: The verse makes an exception for those who cannot go. There is no blame on the blind, the lame or the sick for staying behind from the fighting, since their defects and the causes that hold them back are known to God. One report says God excused those who had a valid excuse, and another says the whole verse concerns the struggle. The verse keeps the summons of the previous verse from becoming a burden no one can carry.

phrases.translation: And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted by Him into Gardens under which rivers flow. But whoever turns away will be subjected by Him to a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: The reward and the punishment are then restated for the ones who could go. Whoever obeys God and His messenger is admitted into gardens beneath which the rivers flow, and whoever turns away is punished with a painful punishment. The obedience here is explained as answering the call to fight when it comes, seeking God's face. The verse closes the passage on the Bedouins by putting the choice in its plainest terms.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree.
phrases.explanation: The verse returns to the pledge itself. God was pleased with the believers when they swore allegiance to the Prophet under the tree, and the pledge is explained as the oath at Ḥudaybiya not to flee and not to turn their backs to the enemy. Reports give the occasion: the Prophet sent Uthman to Quraysh, word came that he had been killed, and the companions were called to swear. The numbers are reported as fourteen hundred, or fifteen hundred, or thirteen hundred.

phrases.translation: He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand
phrases.explanation: God knew what was in their hearts when they swore, and the verse names the response. He sent down serenity upon them, the same calm given to the believers earlier in the surah, and He rewarded them with a victory near at hand. One report notes that they did not swear to die but swore that they would not flee, and that all of them swore except one man who hid behind his camel. The reward answers the sincerity rather than the number.

phrases.translation: and many spoils of war they will gain. For Allah is Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The near victory is then named as spoils. God rewarded the people of the pledge with abundant spoils they would take from the Jews of Khaybar, and He made those spoils exclusive to them, to the exclusion of everyone else. The verse closes by naming God Almighty in His retribution and All-Wise in His disposal of what He made. The reward and the victory are joined, since the spoils were the visible form the near victory took.

phrases.translation: Allah has promised you ˹believers˺ abundant spoils, which you will gain, so He hastened this ˹truce˺ for you.
phrases.explanation: The verse returns to the promise of spoils. God has promised the people of the pledge abundant spoils they will acquire, and He hastened something for them in advance. The reports differ over what was hastened, with Khaybar named by one group and the truce itself by another, and the view taken as stronger is that Khaybar was the hastened reward and the rest of the conquests were deferred. The two gifts are kept distinct so that neither is mistaken for the other.

phrases.translation: And He has held people’s hands back from ˹harming˺ you, so it may be a sign for the believers, and so He may guide you along the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: The other half of the favour is protection. God held back the hands of the people from them, and the reports differ over whose hands, naming the Jews and the families left in Medina or the Quraysh. The holding back is called a sign for the believers, so that they might know that God guards their affairs whether they are present or absent, and it is joined to guidance on a straight path.

phrases.translation: And ˹there are˺ other gains which are beyond your reach that Allah is keeping in store ˹for you˺. For Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation: The verse names what has not yet been taken. There are other gains beyond their reach that God is keeping in store for them, and the reports name Persia and Byzantium, or Khaybar, or Mecca. The word used suggests a city they could not take, and the argument is made that this fits Mecca, since they had striven for it and been turned back. What the verse settles is that the delay is a keeping, not a refusal.

phrases.translation: If the disbelievers were to fight you, they would certainly flee.
phrases.explanation: The verse states what would have happened had the fighting come. If the disbelievers had fought the believers at Mecca, they would have turned their backs and fled. The sentence is put as a certainty, not a possibility, and it answers the fear that had weighed on the companions at Ḥudaybiya. The promise stands whether or not the battle was fought.

phrases.translation: Then they would never find any protector or helper
phrases.explanation: The flight would have led nowhere. They would have found no protector to take up their cause and no helper to stand with them against the believers. The reason given is that God is with the believers, and the party that has God as its helper is never defeated. The verse closes the thought with the picture of an enemy who loses both the field and the support behind him.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ Allah’s way, already long established ˹in the past˺.
phrases.explanation: The verse names the principle behind the promise. This is God's way, already long established with the communities that passed before, and the word for way is explained as a law He ordained among them. The defeat and forsaking of those who fought His friends is not a new decision but the same course repeated. The verse places the events at Ḥudaybiya inside a pattern older than the Quraysh.

phrases.translation: And you will find no change in Allah’s way
phrases.explanation: The pattern does not change. The Prophet is told that he will find no alteration in God's way, since good is repaid with good and disbelief and evildoing with punishment. The word is permanent, and the verse states it in the form of a promise to the one who is being opposed. The surah turns from the particular truce to the settled rule that governs every nation.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes a specific restraint. God held back the hands of the enemy from the believers and the hands of the believers from the enemy in the valley of Ḥudaybiya near Mecca. The reports describe a group of Quraysh sent to circle the Muslim camp and seize someone, who were taken instead and then released. The verse gives the reason for the mercy: God had already given the believers the advantage, so the restraint was not weakness.

phrases.translation: after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with a statement about God's sight. He sees what they do at that place, the pardon they granted when they could have killed, and nothing of it is hidden from Him. The words hold both parties under the same gaze, since the enemy's scheming and the believers' restraint are both seen. The sentence turns a moment of restraint into a deed that is recorded.

phrases.translation: They are the ones who persisted in disbelief and hindered you from the Sacred Mosque, preventing the sacrificial animals from reaching their destination.
phrases.explanation: The verse names what the disbelievers did. They persisted in disbelief, barred the believers from the Sacred Mosque and held back the sacrificial animals so that they could not reach the place of slaughter. The reports describe the camels brought on that journey, seventy of them for seven hundred men, turned away from the sanctuary. The verse states the offence in its plain form before it explains why the believers did not enter.

phrases.translation: ˹We would have let you march through Mecca,˺ had there not been believing men and women, unknown to you. You might have trampled them underfoot, incurring guilt for ˹what you did to˺ them unknowingly. That was so Allah may admit into His mercy whoever He wills.
phrases.explanation: The reason for restraint is then given. There were believing men and women in Mecca unknown to the believers, and had they marched in they might have trampled them, and guilt would have fallen on them without their knowledge. One report takes the guilt as sin and another as the blood money or expiation. God held the believers back so that He might admit into His mercy whom He willed, and the sentence leaves the answer to the condition unspoken because the sense is complete.

phrases.translation: Had those ˹unknown˺ believers stood apart, We would have certainly inflicted a painful punishment on the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with what would have followed a separation. Had those believers stood apart from the disbelievers and left their midst, God would have punished the disbelievers with a painful punishment and given the believers the victory they sought. One report says God wards off through the believers the evil of the disbelievers, so that the few protect the many. The sentence measures the mercy of the delay against the punishment it postponed.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when the disbelievers had filled their hearts with pride—the pride of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance—
phrases.explanation: The verse names the temper of the other side. When the disbelievers filled their hearts with pride, the pride of the age of ignorance, they refused to have the name of the Most Merciful written in the treaty and refused the title of messenger beside the Prophet's name. One report explains the pride as their refusal to acknowledge the words that would have honoured him. The verse calls it the pride of ignorance because nothing in it came from God's permission.

phrases.translation: then Allah sent down His serenity upon His Messenger and the believers, inspiring them to uphold the declaration of faith, for they were better entitled and more worthy of it. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things
phrases.explanation: The answer to that pride is then given. God sent down His serenity upon His messenger and upon the believers, the same calm that steadied them earlier, and He bound them to the word of God-fearingness. The reports explain that word as the declaration that there is no god but God, some adding the formula of His greatness, and another as sincere devotion. The believers were more entitled to it than those who refused it.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah will fulfil His Messenger’s vision in all truth: Allah willing, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in security—˹some with˺ heads shaved and ˹others with˺ hair shortened—without fear.
phrases.explanation: The verse confirms the vision. God will fulfil what He showed His messenger: the believers will enter the Sacred Mosque in security, some with heads shaved and others with hair shortened, without fear. One report describes the companions asking where the vision was when the animals were slaughtered at Ḥudaybiya and they did not enter that year. The verse answers them by saying that the fulfilment is certain and that the delay did not cancel it.

phrases.translation: He knew what you did not know, so He first granted you the triumph at hand
phrases.explanation: The reason for the delay is then named. God knew what they did not know, and what He knew was the believing men and women in Mecca whom the believers could not distinguish. Had they entered, they would have trampled them unknowingly, so the entry was deferred until the hidden believers could be brought out. The verse joins that knowledge to the near victory already granted, so the postponement itself becomes part of the mercy.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who has sent His Messenger with ˹right˺ guidance and the religion of truth, making it prevail over all others.
phrases.explanation: The verse names the purpose of the sending. God has sent His messenger with guidance and with the religion of truth so that it may prevail over every other religion. One report says this will be complete when Jesus descends and all creeds are abolished except the religion with which Muhammad was sent. The promise is stated as something God will accomplish rather than something the believers must secure.

phrases.translation: And sufficient is Allah as a Witness
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with a witness. God is enough as a witness to His own promise, and the report explains the words as God calling the Prophet to take his Lord as witness over Himself that He will make the religion prevail. The verse is a consolation to those who grieved over the terms at Ḥudaybiya, since the outcome is guaranteed by the One who cannot fail. The witness is the guarantee, and the promise rests on it.

phrases.translation: Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah. And those with him are firm with the disbelievers and compassionate with one another. You see them bowing and prostrating ˹in prayer˺, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure. The sign ˹of brightness can be seen˺ on their faces from the trace of prostrating ˹in prayer˺.
phrases.explanation: The surah closes with a portrait of the community. Muhammad is the messenger of God, and those with him are harsh against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. They are seen bowing and prostrating, seeking God's bounty and His good pleasure, and their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration. The mark is explained as a radiance on the Day of Resurrection or as the humility seen in this life, and the stronger view is that it belongs to every time.

phrases.translation: This is their description in the Torah. And their parable in the Gospel is that of a seed that sprouts its ˹tiny˺ branches, making it strong. Then it becomes thick, standing firmly on its stem, to the delight of the planters—in this way Allah makes the believers a source of dismay for the disbelievers.
phrases.explanation: The two scriptures are then called as witnesses. This is their description in the Torah, and in the Gospel they are like a crop that brings out its shoot, which strengthens it until it becomes thick and stands firm on its stalks, to the delight of those who sowed it. The image is explained as the growth of the community from few to many and from weakness to firmness. The purpose is named at the end: that God may enrage the disbelievers through them.

phrases.translation: To those of them who believe and do good, Allah has promised forgiveness and a great reward
phrases.explanation: The verse ends with the promise to those who believe. God has promised those among them who believe and do good deeds forgiveness and a great reward, and the reward is explained as Paradise. The words those among them are read as referring to the later growth of the community, so that the promise reaches everyone who enters the faith until the Day of Resurrection. The surah closes on the two things the whole passage has been aiming at, pardon and reward.
